messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ama was twenty years old and worked behind the counter of a chain pharmacy in a midwestern suburb, counting pills and checking interactions, but her mind lived elsewhere—in a flooded basement in the country she had fled two years earlier. There, during the political unrest that tore through her town, she had been taken by armed men who accused her family of harboring rebels. For three days they kept her in a room that filled with water whenever it rained. They forced her head under the murky surface until her lungs burned, then pulled her up to scream questions she could not answer. She remembered the weight of a boot on the back of her neck, the metallic taste of silt, the sight of another prisoner being dragged away—a woman whose name she never learned. Ama survived because she was young and because the men grew bored, but the woman did not. That guilt sat inside her like a stone.

In the months after her escape and resettlement, Ama began to notice that certain things could pull her back into that basement without warning. The sight of a full sink at work, or a customer’s glass of water, would make her breath catch. Arguments with her boyfriend over small things—whose turn to cook, why she was late—would trigger a cold panic, because being forced into a corner felt identical to being forced underwater. And when a manager pressured her to stay late, she felt the same helplessness, the same rage. Each time one of these triggers appeared, she found herself slipping into fragments of memory: her body would tense into the exact arched position she had held when the water covered her face, even as she stood dry and safe behind the pharmacy counter. She could never remember the whole sequence—only flashes of cold, pressure, and the sound of shouting. She could not put the event into words; when her boyfriend asked what had happened to her, she would shake her head and say nothing, because the story had no language.

Ama had come to believe that she had to be on guard all the time, that if she relaxed for a single moment something terrible would catch her unaware. This hypervigilance meant that she scanned every customer who entered the pharmacy, noting exits and blind spots. She avoided the break room because it had no second door. When she tried to sleep at night, she lay rigid, listening for footsteps on the stairs, her body refusing to surrender to unconsciousness because being asleep felt too much like being underwater. She told herself she deserved this suffering—that she had survived when the other woman did not, so she had no right to rest. This punishment thinking kept her trapped in a loop: the more she believed she should suffer, the more she watched for danger, and the more she watched for danger, the more she noticed triggers. A bag of ice melting on the counter would become a flood. A raised voice from a customer would become an interrogation.

She had developed a set of habits to manage the terror. She avoided the hour before dawn because that was when the nightmares came most vividly, and she was certain that if she let one of those dreams take hold, she would not be able to recover. She avoided coworkers who had dark skin and a particular build—men who reminded her of the guards—and she knew this was irrational, but she could not help it. Whenever a memory surfaced, she pushed it away immediately, telling herself that if she started to think about the event, she would fall apart completely and never pull herself back together. This thought avoidance meant that the memories stayed fragmented, nonverbal, locked in her body but unreachable by words. The incomplete picture haunted her more than the flood itself: she could feel the water in her lungs but could not remember how she got out.

The cycles had tightened over the past year. Her boyfriend had started to pull away, confused by her abrupt silences and her refusal to go to the lake or even to the pool at the gym. At work, she had begun mapping escape routes in every room, scanning the parking lot for cars that looked out of place, and her concentration suffered. A customer complained that she seemed distracted. Her manager suggested she take a leave of absence. That was what finally brought her to a clinic: the fear that she was losing the one thing she had built after escaping. But what frightened her most was the thought that, if she stopped being vigilant for even a moment, the water would find her again. She hoped—barely—that talking to someone might help her find the words she had lost.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not show that negative appraisals (e.g., guilt, deserving suffering) directly cause or lead to trauma memories.
The vignette does not convey that a sense of threat causes or elicits trauma memories.
The vignette does not indicate that maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance, hypervigilance) cause or increase a sense of threat.
